passages.text: HAYKALAH takes real estate from raw land to an income-producing asset. The practice serves landowners, developers, family offices and government entities, drawing on a record that runs from central Makkah and the Holy Sites to downtown Jeddah.

passages.section: What is Musataha, and how is it used in Saudi real estate?
passages.text: Musataha is a right to build on and use land owned by another party for an agreed term. The landowner keeps title while a project company builds and runs the asset. An Ijara or a Sukuk structure can sit on top of it.

passages.section: Can landowners contribute land instead of cash?
passages.text: Yes. In an in-kind contribution the land is valued and exchanged for equity in the project company. HAYKALAH has modeled this in central Makkah, where landowners’ land formed part of the project’s capital.

passages.section: What is the difference between a family waqf and a charitable waqf?
passages.text: A family waqf directs its income to the founder’s family and descendants. A charitable waqf directs it to charitable or public purposes. A joint waqf does both, in the shares the waqf deed sets.
The nazir administers a waqf. The nazir manages its assets, collects the income and distributes it to the beneficiaries as the waqf deed requires.

passages.section: How are Sukuk different from conventional bonds?
passages.text: Sukuk give holders a share in an underlying asset or its returns. The return comes from the asset, for example rent under an Ijara, rather than from interest on a loan.
A lease-based Sukuk. An SPV holds the leased asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, and the rent paid by the lessee funds the periodic distributions.

Monetize: recurring income, refinancing and capital recycling. Revenue-share agreements in which HAYKALAH earns from the income the asset produces.

passages.text: What room rates a hotel can expect through the year. With occupancy, the rates set the hotel’s revenue and the debt it can carry.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.text: HAYKALAH proposed this framework in 2026. It is a proposal with no mandate, and its figures are withheld until the source documents are reconciled. A stadium needs capital long before it earns. In 2026 HAYKALAH proposed a Sukuk framework for stadium precincts that combines three Shariah contracts: Musataha rights over the land, Istisna’a during construction, then Ijara or Wakala-Ijara once the stadium is complete. There is one issuer per stadium, across seven precincts for 2034. This explainer steps through the framework as proposed. It is a proposal, not a mandate.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.section: The issuer takes Musataha rights over the land.
passages.text: The landowner grants the issuer the right to build on and use the land for an agreed term, and keeps title throughout. The framework proposes one issuer for each stadium.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.section: A Shariah board approves the structure.
passages.text: Before any Sukuk are issued, a Shariah board reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents. HAYKALAH does not maintain its own Shariah board; where the issuer has none, HAYKALAH can arrange an independent one.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.text: The issuer orders the stadium to an agreed specification under an Istisna’a, and the price can be paid in stages while it is built. The contractor who builds it can work under a separate, parallel Istisna’a.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.text: Once the stadium is complete, it moves to an Ijara, or to a Wakala-Ijara in which an agent procures the asset that is then leased. The lessee pays rent for the use of the stadium, and the issuer, as lessor, keeps the responsibilities of ownership that the contract and the applicable Shariah standards assign to it.

passages.page: Stadium Sukuk (Proposal): How It Would Work
passages.section: The rent pays the Sukuk holders.
passages.text: The rent funds periodic distributions to the Sukuk holders. The landowner keeps title to the land throughout, and the Musataha contract sets what happens to the buildings when its term ends.

Shariah board. Reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents. Licensed institution. Offers the Sukuk to investors, a regulated activity

The Musataha runs for an agreed term, and its contract sets what happens to the buildings when the term ends. No guarantee of approvals, financing or returns.

Land, buildings and facilities that cost money to hold can be audited, re-planned, structured and operated to earn recurring income. passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.text: This explainer describes the general structure of Sukuk al-Ijara. It is not a HAYKALAH transaction, and the terms of each issue vary. Sukuk al-Ijara are lease-based Sukuk. A special purpose vehicle holds a leased asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, and the rent paid by the lessee funds the periodic distributions. Each issue rests on Ijara, a Shariah-compliant lease in which the owner of an asset lets another party use it for an agreed term in return for an agreed rent. This explainer follows a typical issue from the asset to maturity.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.section: The originator chooses an asset that can be leased.
passages.text: The issue starts with an asset that earns, or can earn, rent, such as a building or equipment. Its title and documents have to be in order, because the Sukuk rest on it.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.section: An SPV is set up, and the structure is approved.
passages.text: A special purpose vehicle is set up to hold the asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, usually acting as their trustee. A Shariah board reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents before the issue.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.section: The holders pay for the Sukuk, and the asset moves to the SPV.
passages.text: Investors buy the Sukuk through an appropriately licensed institution, because offering Sukuk is a regulated activity. The SPV uses the proceeds to buy the asset from the originator.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.section: The SPV leases the asset under an Ijara.
passages.text: The SPV leases the asset, often back to the originator, for an agreed term and rent. As lessor, the SPV keeps the responsibilities of ownership that the contract and the applicable Shariah standards assign to it.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.text: The lessee pays rent on the agreed dates, and the SPV passes it to the Sukuk holders as periodic distributions. Their return comes from the rent, not from interest on a loan.

passages.page: Sukuk al-Ijara: How Lease-Based Sukuk Work
passages.section: At maturity, the originator buys the asset back.
passages.text: At the end of the term, the originator usually buys the asset back under a separate promise given at the start. The SPV pays the price to the Sukuk holders, and the Sukuk end.

passages.page: Sukuk: What They Are and How They Work
passages.text: Also called: Islamic certificates; singular sakk. Sukuk are Shariah-compliant certificates that represent an undivided share in an underlying asset, project or business activity, or in its returns.

passages.page: Sukuk: What They Are and How They Work
passages.text: A conventional bond is a loan: the holder is paid interest on a debt. Sukuk work differently. The holders own a share in an asset or an activity, and their return comes from it, for example from the rent paid under an Ijara lease. Each Sukuk issue is built on one or more Shariah contracts, such as Ijara, Istisna’a, Musataha, Wakala, Murabaha or Musharaka. A special purpose vehicle usually holds the asset on behalf of the holders and passes its income to them. The contracts, the asset and the documents are reviewed and approved by a Shariah board before the issue.

passages.page: Sukuk: What They Are and How They Work
passages.text: Offering Sukuk to investors and dealing in them are regulated activities, executed through appropriately licensed partners.

passages.page: Sukuk: What They Are and How They Work

In 2025 it prepared three income-producing assets in Riyadh for Sukuk and tokenization, with a 34-point proofing checklist, a data-room design and screening bands (early stage). It has also prepared a housing Sukuk program with an optional tokenized slice (a proposal) and proposed a Sukuk framework for stadium precincts (a proposal with no mandate). Also called: Ijarah; Sukuk al-Ijara. Ijara is a Shariah-compliant lease in which the owner of an asset lets another party use it for an agreed term in return for an agreed rent.

In an Ijara the lessor keeps ownership of the asset, with the responsibilities of ownership that the contract and the applicable Shariah standards assign to it. The lessee pays rent for the use of the asset. What is sold is the use of the asset, not the asset itself. A common form ends with ownership passing to the lessee at the end of the term, through a separate promise or sale. Banks use it to finance homes, equipment and buildings.
In Sukuk al-Ijara, a special purpose vehicle holds the leased asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, and the rent paid by the lessee funds the periodic distributions.

Ijara is one of the contracts FINA. builds Sukuk on, and one of the structures HAYKALAH uses to put idle land and buildings to work for recurring income. In the stadium precinct Sukuk framework that HAYKALAH proposed in 2026, the completed stadium is leased under an Ijara whose rent pays the Sukuk holders; the framework is a proposal with no mandate. For a family with idle land, a lease is one option alongside a joint venture, a Musataha or an in-kind contribution.

Also called: Istisna; Istisnaa. Istisna’a is a Shariah-compliant contract to manufacture or build a specified asset for an agreed price, with delivery at a future date.

In an Istisna’a, the buyer orders an asset that does not exist yet, such as a building, a plant or equipment, to an agreed specification. The price is fixed in the contract and can be paid in stages, including while the asset is being built. This makes Istisna’a a common way to fund construction. A financier can agree an Istisna’a with the client and a separate, parallel Istisna’a with the contractor who builds the asset. Once the asset is complete, it is often leased under an Ijara, so that the construction phase and the income phase sit in one structure.

Istisna’a is one of the contracts FINA. builds Sukuk on. HAYKALAH’s Sukuk frameworks for public assets combine Musataha, Istisna’a and Ijara, with one issuer per asset. In the stadium precinct framework it proposed in 2026, Istisna’a funds construction before the completed stadium is leased under an Ijara; the framework is a proposal with no mandate.

Also called: Murabahah; cost-plus sale. Murabaha is a Shariah-compliant sale in which the seller discloses what an asset cost and sells it at that cost plus an agreed profit, often with payment deferred.

In a Murabaha used for financing, a bank buys the asset a client needs and then sells it to the client at its cost plus a disclosed profit. The client pays the price in installments over an agreed period. The profit is part of the sale price and is agreed at the outset; it is not interest on a loan. For the sale to be valid, the seller must own the asset, and carry the risk of owning it, before selling it on. Banks use Murabaha widely for asset and trade finance.

Murabaha is one of the Shariah contracts that FINA. and HAYKALAH’s work with banks draw on. In HAYKALAH’s method the contract follows from the asset and its cash flows, not the other way round, and the institution’s own Shariah board approves the structure.

Also called: Musharakah; diminishing Musharaka. Musharaka is a Shariah-compliant partnership in which two or more parties contribute capital to a venture, share its profit as agreed and bear its losses in proportion to their capital.

Each partner holds a stake in the venture rather than a claim to a fixed return. Profit is shared in the ratios the partners agree; losses are shared in proportion to the capital each partner put in. In a diminishing Musharaka, one partner buys the other’s share step by step until it owns the whole asset. Banks use this form for home and asset finance. Musharaka can also be the basis of a Sukuk issue.

Musharaka is among the structures HAYKALAH lists for FINA., for venture building and for international companies forming joint ventures in the Kingdom: settings in which partners share a venture’s risk and reward. As an institutional co-founder, HAYKALAH takes part of its reward as equity, so it shares the venture’s risk alongside the founders.

Also called: Wakalah; agency; Wakala-Ijara. Wakala is a Shariah-compliant agency contract in which one party, the principal, appoints another, the agent or wakil, to act on its behalf, usually for an agreed fee.

The agent acts within the mandate the principal gives it and is paid a fee agreed in advance. In an investment Wakala, the agent invests the principal’s funds in Shariah-compliant activities on the principal’s behalf. In a Wakala Sukuk, an agent manages a pool of Shariah-compliant assets for the Sukuk holders. Wakala is also combined with Ijara, so that an agent procures an asset that is then leased.

Wakala is one of the contracts FINA. builds Sukuk on, and part of HAYKALAH’s Sukuk and fund templates. In the stadium precinct Sukuk framework it proposed in 2026, the completed stadium moves to an Ijara or a Wakala-Ijara; the framework is a proposal with no mandate.

passages.page: JV SPV: Joint-Venture Special Purpose Vehicle
passages.text: Also called: joint-venture special purpose vehicle. A JV SPV is a company that two or more partners form for a single project or asset, so that the project’s ownership, finance and risk sit apart from the partners’ other businesses.

passages.page: JV SPV: Joint-Venture Special Purpose Vehicle
passages.text: SPV stands for special purpose vehicle: a company set up to do one thing, such as own a building or run a project. JV stands for joint venture: two or more partners owning that company together. A shareholders’ agreement sets out what each partner contributes, how decisions are made and how a partner can leave.

passages.page: JV SPV: Joint-Venture Special Purpose Vehicle
passages.text: Because the project sits in its own company, lenders and investors can assess it on its own assets and cash flows. A landowner can join by contributing land in kind, and an operator or an investor by contributing cash or expertise.

passages.page: JV SPV: Joint-Venture Special Purpose Vehicle
passages.text: HAYKALAH designs SPV and joint-venture structures for real estate, for family-owned land and for international companies entering the Kingdom with a Saudi partner. In the asset-monetization engine, a JV SPV is one of the structures that can put an under-used asset to work. For sports facilities, HAYKALAH designed a shared-access joint venture and concession SPVs (a framework, 2025–26).

Also called: development company and project company. A DevCo/ProjectCo structure pairs one permanent development company, which holds a consortium’s origination, studies and know-how, with a separate project company formed for each tender or project.

The development company, or DevCo, is permanent. It keeps what the consortium learns from one bid to the next: its origination, studies, relationships and know-how. For each tender or project, the consortium forms a separate project company, or ProjectCo, with its own capital, contracts and financing.

The lead member of each ProjectCo can change to suit the tender, and each project’s risks stay inside its own company. The structure suits public-private partnerships, where one consortium may bid for several tenders over time.

DevCo/ProjectCo consortium architecture is one of HAYKALAH’s domain playbooks: pooling land from many owners, allocating risk, and the consortium rules of the PSP Law. In 2026 HAYKALAH convened a five-party consortium for smart industrial-city PPPs, with a permanent DevCo and a ProjectCo for each tender, and as DevCo lead prepared its profile, roles annex and heads of terms; the consortium is in formation. Since 2024, HAYKALAH’s commercial model has included DevCo stakes.

passages.page: Holding Companies for Families and Groups
passages.text: Also called: holding structure. A holding company is a company whose main purpose is to own shares in other companies, so that ownership and control sit above the operating businesses.

passages.page: Holding Companies for Families and Groups
passages.text: For a family or a group, a holding company separates ownership from management. The family owns the holding company; the holding company owns the operating companies and the assets; each operating company has its own management. Governance can then be set at one level: the holding company’s board, the decisions reserved to the owners, and the reports each business sends up. Succession becomes a question of who holds the holding company’s shares, rather than a separate transfer of every asset. The rules for forming and running a holding company depend on the jurisdiction.

passages.page: Holding Companies for Families and Groups
passages.text: HAYKALAH designs holding structures that separate ownership, management and the operating companies for family offices, trusts and family-owned groups, and it sets ownership, governance and succession together, with a holding company or a waqf where each fits. Holding companies also appear in HAYKALAH’s venture builds and in the entities that international companies use to enter the Kingdom.

passages.page: Real-Estate Funds in Saudi Arabia Explained
passages.text: Also called: real-estate investment fund. A real-estate fund is an investment fund that pools investors’ money to own, develop or finance real estate, under the terms set out in the fund’s documents.

passages.page: Real-Estate Funds in Saudi Arabia Explained
passages.text: Investors buy units in the fund, and the fund holds the real estate. A fund manager runs the fund under its terms and conditions, and a fund board oversees it. A fund can be private, for a limited group of investors, or offered to the public. In the Kingdom, establishing and managing an investment fund is a regulated activity, carried out by a fund manager authorised by the Capital Market Authority. Income-producing assets with a record of occupancy and rent suit a fund, because their cash flows can be assessed.

passages.page: Real-Estate Funds in Saudi Arabia Explained
passages.text: HAYKALAH designs fund structures and term sheets, with each fund set up and managed by a CMA-authorised manager. In real estate, a fund is one of the vehicles that can hold land and buildings once they earn; in the asset-monetization engine, a fund or Sukuk is the route at scale. HAYKALAH does not establish or manage investment funds.

Also called: off-balance-sheet SPV. An off-balance-sheet vehicle is a separate entity that holds assets, and often the financing behind them, outside the sponsor’s own balance sheet, where the accounting rules allow it.

The vehicle is usually a special purpose company that owns the asset and raises the financing for it. Lenders and investors look to the vehicle’s own assets and cash flows, so the project’s risk is kept apart from the sponsor’s other business. Whether the vehicle actually stays off the sponsor’s balance sheet is decided under the applicable accounting standards, which look at who controls it. The name of the structure does not decide it, so the auditors’ view is needed early.
Off-balance-sheet vehicles are part of FINA., HAYKALAH’s financial structuring practice, alongside asset-backed securitization, Sukuk and joint-venture structures.

Also called: asset-backed securities. Securitization turns a pool of income-producing assets or receivables into securities that investors can buy, with payments on those securities funded by the pool’s cash flows.

The owner of the assets, often called the originator, transfers them to a special purpose vehicle. The vehicle issues securities to investors and pays them from what the assets earn, such as rent or receivables. The assets are kept apart from the originator’s other business. In Islamic finance, asset-backed Sukuk play a similar role, subject to Shariah rules on what can be sold and how. Offering the resulting securities to investors is a regulated activity, executed through appropriately licensed partners.

Asset-backed securitization is part of FINA., HAYKALAH’s financial structuring practice, and of its work with banks, alongside Sukuk and off-balance-sheet vehicles. HAYKALAH’s Sukuk and fund templates include asset-backed Sukuk.
Also called: asset tokenization. Tokenization records rights in an asset, such as ownership or a share of its income, as digital tokens on a digital ledger.

A token is a digital record of a right. Tokenization can divide an asset into smaller units and keep the record of who holds them in digital form. Before an asset can be tokenized, its documents, title and data have to be in order, because the tokens are only as reliable as the records behind them.

HAYKALAH prepares assets for tokenization; it does not issue, offer or deal in tokens. In 2025, for three income-producing assets in Riyadh, it prepared a 34-point proofing checklist, a data-room design and screening bands ahead of Sukuk and tokenization (early stage). It has also prepared a housing Sukuk program with an optional tokenized slice, a proposal with a collaboration MoU signed in January 2026, and it designs investment-platform architecture for tokenized offerings.

Also called: Islamic endowment; family waqf; charitable waqf. A waqf is an Islamic endowment in which an owner dedicates an asset permanently so that its income goes to the beneficiaries named in the waqf deed.

The founder of a waqf dedicates an asset, such as land or a building, so that the asset itself is preserved and its income is used for the purposes the founder sets. The waqf deed names the beneficiaries and the rules for running the waqf. A family waqf directs its income to the founder’s family and descendants. A charitable waqf directs it to charitable or public purposes. A joint waqf does both, in the shares the waqf deed sets.
A nazir administers the waqf. In the Kingdom, waqfs are subject to oversight by the competent authority.

HAYKALAH has structured waqfs since 2010 and codified the work into a waqf-manager model: establishing the waqf, governing it through a nazir and distributing its income. In 2021 it proposed a family and charitable waqf for a Saudi family, with a nine-month plan to establish it, coordinate its legal, Shariah and accounting advisers and seat the first nazir board (proposed). NATHARAH is a HAYKALAH venture built on the waqf-manager model.
Shariah structures are subject to Shariah board approval. Clients are not named until they consent.

Also called: waqf administrator; nazir board. The nazir is the person or body that administers a waqf, managing its assets, collecting its income and distributing it as the waqf deed requires.

The waqf deed usually names the nazir and says how a successor is chosen. A nazir can be an individual, a board or an institution. The nazir holds the waqf’s assets in trust: it must preserve them, follow the founder’s conditions and act in the beneficiaries’ interest. For a larger waqf, a nazir board with clear decision rights, accounts and regular reports makes the waqf easier to run and to check.

Nazir governance is part of HAYKALAH’s family and charitable waqf design and of its waqf-manager model, together with establishing the waqf and distributing its income. HAYKALAH’s 2021 waqf proposal for a Saudi family included seating the first nazir board.

passages.page: Musataha: The Right to Build on Land
passages.text: Also called: right to build; surface right. Musataha is a right to build on and use land owned by another party for an agreed term, while the landowner keeps title to the land.

passages.page: Musataha: The Right to Build on Land
passages.text: The landowner grants the right, and a project company builds the asset and runs it for the term of the Musataha. The landowner keeps title throughout, and the contract sets what happens to the buildings when the term ends. Musataha lets public and private landowners put land to work without selling it. An Ijara or a Sukuk structure can sit on top of it, so that the rights over the land, the construction and the income are financed together.

passages.page: Musataha: The Right to Build on Land
passages.text: HAYKALAH uses Musataha in real-estate structuring, in its Sukuk frameworks for public assets, and in the asset-monetization engine as one way to put idle land to work. In the stadium precinct Sukuk framework it proposed in 2026, the issuer takes Musataha rights over the land, funds construction through Istisna’a and then leases the stadium under an Ijara; the framework is a proposal with no mandate.

Also called: contribution in kind; land for equity. An in-kind contribution is a non-cash asset, such as land, that a partner contributes to a company in exchange for shares, at an agreed valuation.

The asset is valued, and the contributor receives shares in the company equal to that value. Landowners become equity partners in the project instead of selling their land, and the project needs less cash at the start. The valuation is the central question, because it sets each partner’s share. Where many owners contribute small plots, an in-kind structure can assemble a site that no single owner could develop alone.

HAYKALAH structures land assembly through in-kind contributions, so that landowners join the project as equity partners. Central-area land assembly with in-kind equity is part of its Holy Cities land-to-asset playbook. In 2009, for a mixed-use development on about 151,000 m² of central Makkah, the structure modeled landowners’ land as an in-kind contribution to the project’s capital.

Also called: concession contract. A concession is a contract that gives a party the right to operate an asset or a service for a set term, in return for payments or a share of the revenue.

The owner, often a public body, keeps ownership of the asset. The concessionaire invests in it, operates it and earns from it during the term, then hands it back as the contract requires. The contract sets the term, the payments or the revenue share, the performance standards and the condition in which the asset is returned. Concessions are common for venues, transport and utilities, and in public-private partnerships.

A concession is one of the structures in HAYKALAH’s asset-monetization engine, which moves owners from building and selling to owning, optimizing and earning through leases, concessions and revenue share. For sports facilities, HAYKALAH designed a shared-access joint venture and concession SPVs to turn under-used stadiums and facilities into event, lease and activation income (a framework, 2025–26).

Also called: revenue-share agreement. A revenue share is an agreement under which a party receives an agreed percentage of the revenue an asset or business produces, instead of, or in addition to, a fixed fee or rent.

Instead of a fixed amount, the payment rises and falls with the revenue, so the parties share an interest in the asset performing well. Operators, landlords and advisers can all be paid this way. The agreement has to define revenue precisely, say how it is measured and reported, and set when payments are made.

In HAYKALAH’s asset-monetization engine, a revenue share is one of the structures that let an owner earn from an asset instead of selling it. HAYKALAH can itself earn through revenue-share agreements: fees, a share of the revenue the asset generates, or both, agreed asset by asset.

Also called: asset recycling. Capital recycling is releasing capital from an asset once it earns, through refinancing or a sale, and reinvesting that capital in the next asset.

An asset with steady income can support new financing, or attract a buyer or a fund. The owner uses that to take out part of the capital invested, rather than leaving it tied up in one asset, and puts it to work on the next one. The cycle depends on records that lenders and investors trust: a history of income, an up-to-date model and complete documents.

Capital recycling is the last step of HAYKALAH’s asset-monetization engine, Audit → Optimize → Structure → Operate → Monetize: recurring income supports refinancing, and released capital moves to the next asset. Monetization, one of HAYKALAH’s six ways of creating value, turns idle land, buildings and facilities into income, refinancing capacity and capital to recycle.

Also called: co-founder equity. Equity-for-build is a model in which HAYKALAH takes part of its reward as equity in the company or project it builds, vesting at agreed milestones, instead of fees alone.

The co-founder’s equity vests in stages, tied to milestones such as registration, the first revenue contract and a KPI threshold. Equity for a milestone that is not reached does not vest. The model ties the co-founder’s reward to the venture’s progress. It can be combined with a retainer or a success fee, and fees can be deferred into project equity.

Also called: milestone vesting. Vesting is the process by which shares or other rights promised to a person become theirs in stages, as agreed conditions such as time or milestones are met.

Until a share vests, the holder cannot keep it if the agreed condition is not met. Vesting can depend on time, such as a number of years with the company, or on milestones, such as a registration, a first contract or a performance threshold. Milestone vesting works when each milestone is defined clearly enough that everyone can agree whether it was reached. The rules usually sit in the shareholders’ agreement.

In HAYKALAH’s venture builds, equity vests at gates agreed when the company is formed, for example 20% at registration, 30% at the first revenue contract and 50% at an agreed KPI threshold. That split comes from the Saudi-German localization engine, a final draft in which a partner pool of 25% of each Saudi entity vests in those stages.

Also called: shareholder agreement. A shareholders’ agreement is a contract among a company’s shareholders that sets how the company is owned, governed and funded, and how shareholders can enter or leave.

It usually covers board seats and the decisions reserved to shareholders, how new shares are issued and existing shares transferred, how deadlocks are resolved, what each shareholder must fund, and how a shareholder can exit. Vesting rules for founders often sit here too. It works alongside the company’s articles of association, and it must be consistent with the law of the place where the company is registered.

Shareholders’ agreements are part of the governance HAYKALAH puts in place in its venture builds, together with boards and trackers for conditions precedent. For international companies entering the Kingdom, HAYKALAH structures the entity and its terms: ownership, roles, vesting gates and exit.

passages.page: PDPL: Saudi Personal Data Protection Law
passages.text: Also called: Personal Data Protection Law. The PDPL is the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law, which sets how personal data may be collected, used, shared and kept, and is overseen by the Saudi Data & AI Authority (SDAIA).

passages.page: PDPL: Saudi Personal Data Protection Law
passages.text: The law gives individuals rights over their personal data, such as the right to be told how it is used, to access it, and to ask for it to be corrected or destroyed. An organization that processes personal data needs a lawful basis, such as consent; must tell people how their data is used; must keep it secure; and must meet conditions before transferring it outside the Kingdom. Implementing regulations set out the detail.

passages.page: PSP Law: Saudi Private Sector Participation
passages.text: Also called: Private Sector Participation Law. The PSP Law is the Saudi Private Sector Participation Law, which sets the rules for public-private partnerships and privatization in the Kingdom.

passages.page: PSP Law: Saudi Private Sector Participation
passages.text: In a public-private partnership, a private partner designs, builds, finances, operates or maintains a public asset or service under a long-term contract, and the risks are shared between the public and the private sides. Privatization moves the ownership or the management of a public asset or service to the private sector.

passages.page: PSP Law: Saudi Private Sector Participation
passages.text: The law sets how such projects are prepared, tendered and contracted, and which competent authority approves them. This is a general description of the law, not legal advice.
